n0001.title: Cargo Cult Science
n0001.gist: Science is more than following its outward rituals; without strict self-honesty, a field can look scientific yet never actually work.
n0001.question: Cargo cult science — what separates real science from empty imitation of its forms? (a governing principle)

n0002.title: What Is Cargo Cult Science
n0002.gist: Feynman surveys popular pseudosciences and failed social 'sciences' before naming the shared flaw: these fields copy science's form but, like a cargo-cult runway, never make anything real land.
n0002.question: Pseudoscience — why do fields that look scientific still fail to work? (several examples, then a definition)

n0003.title: Title and framing
n0003.gist: The talk is introduced as Feynman's 1974 Caltech commencement remarks on science, pseudoscience, and how not to fool yourself.

n0008.title: Investigating mysticism and ESP
n0008.gist: Feynman describes personally testing isolation tanks, Esalen-style mysticism, and Uri Geller's claimed key-bending, finding nothing that actually worked under scrutiny.

n0014.title: Pseudoscience in education and crime
n0014.gist: Despite being treated as scientific, methods for teaching reading and handling criminals show no real improvement over time, resembling the failed remedies of witch doctors.

n0018.title: Cocktail party test
n0018.gist: Feynman proposes a half-joking test for undiscovered pseudosciences: any topic you can discuss at a party without seeming to be talking shop is one nobody truly understands.

n0021.title: Cargo Cult Science
n0021.gist: Like South Sea islanders building fake airstrips that never bring planes, these fields follow all the forms of science yet are missing something essential, so they do not work.

n0023.title: Scientific Integrity
n0023.gist: Real science demands leaning over backwards to report every fact that might undermine your own result, not only the evidence that supports it, which is what cargo cult science lacks.
n0023.question: Scientific integrity — what is the missing ingredient in cargo cult science? (a definition and examples)

n0024.title: Reporting all the evidence
n0024.gist: True scientific integrity means disclosing every detail that could throw doubt on your results and every fact that disagrees with your theory, not just the favorable ones.

n0027.title: Advertising versus integrity
n0027.gist: The goal is to give all information needed to judge your work fairly; contrasted with advertising's true-but-misleading claims, like Wesson Oil's accurate yet deceptive statement about soaking through food.

n0030.title: Truth eventually comes out
n0030.gist: Other experimenters will eventually test your claims against nature, so lacking integrity costs real scientific reputation even if it is not the only reason cargo cult science fails.

n0033.title: Learning from Millikan's Error
n0033.gist: The slow, embarrassing drift of measured electron-charge values after Millikan's flawed experiment shows how scientists once unconsciously filtered out results that disagreed with an authority's number.
n0033.question: Millikan's electron-charge measurement — how did scientists learn to stop fooling themselves? (a historical case)

n0034.title: The drifting electron charge
n0034.gist: After Millikan's oil-drop experiment gave a slightly wrong value for the electron's charge, later measurements crept upward only gradually, because researchers distrusted results too far from his number and dug harder to find fault with them, delaying correction.

n0037.title: A lesson not formally taught
n0037.gist: This history of unconsciously biased measurement taught scientists a trick for avoiding self-deception, yet it remains something students absorb by osmosis rather than through any explicit course.

n0039.title: Honesty Toward the Public
n0039.gist: Scientists owe the public the same bending-over-backwards honesty they owe each other, including admitting when research has no practical application and publishing results regardless of which way they come out.
n0039.question: Scientific honesty toward laymen — what extra duty does a scientist owe the public? (two cases)

n0040.title: Not fooling the layman
n0040.gist: Beyond not fooling yourself, a scientist should not mislead ordinary people either, as when a researcher considered overstating an application of his cosmology work just to secure funding.

n0044.title: Publishing every result
n0044.gist: Integrity requires publishing results whichever way they come out, whether in research on a product like low-nicotine cigarettes or in scientific advice given to politicians, since selective publication misleads just as advertising does.

n0047.title: Examples of Poor Science
n0047.gist: Case studies from psychology and physics show how skipping control experiments, chasing quick results, or ignoring inconvenient rigor produces findings that are not really science at all.
n0047.question: Poor scientific practice — what mistakes keep research from being genuine science? (four case studies)

n0048.title: Skipping the control experiment
n0048.gist: A psychology student's professor forbade her from first repeating an earlier rat experiment under the original conditions before changing them, a 1930s policy that left her unable to know whether her new result truly came from her change.

n0052.title: Pressure for new results in physics
n0052.gist: At a major accelerator lab, pressure to produce new results for funding led researchers to compare their heavy-hydrogen data to someone else's light-hydrogen experiment rather than run the matching test themselves, undermining the point of the experiment.

n0054.title: Young's rat-running experiment
n0054.gist: Psychologist Young painstakingly eliminated every possible cue—sight, smell, sound, even floor texture—before concluding rats really could not be trained to a fixed door, producing a model experiment that later researchers simply ignored.

n0060.title: Shrinking ESP effects
n0060.gist: As critics pressed parapsychologists like Rhine to tighten their methods, the measured ESP effects kept shrinking toward nothing, yet researchers still resisted demanding a reliably repeatable experiment as real science would.

n0063.title: Closing Wish
n0063.gist: Feynman closes by wishing graduates the freedom to keep scientific integrity even under pressure from institutions or funding, and to never promise a talk without knowing what to say.
